procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (inferred from the High Court appeal being against a conviction and sentence)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 27.09.2012 passed by the Allahabad High Court upholding the conviction of the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant, along with others, filed Criminal Appeal No. 340 of 1997 before the Allahabad High Court under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) challenging their conviction and sentence. The High Court, via judgment and order dated 27.09.2012, affirmed the conviction and sentence and dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed a Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (SLP(Criminal) No. 750/2013) before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court issued notice on the SLP and the application for bail on 04.02.2013. On 30.06.2014, the Supreme Court granted leave to appeal but rejected the prayer for bail, leading to the registration of Criminal Appeal No. 1348 of 2014. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution could prove the charges against the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC beyond reasonable doubt.

facts: The appellant was convicted under Sections 148 and 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for the murder of his uncle.
Two eyewitnesses (PW-1 and PW-2, the sons of the deceased) testified that the appellant was present at the scene of the crime.
According to the witnesses, the appellant was carrying a country-made pistol.

The specific role attributed to the appellant was not that he shot the deceased, but that he fired his pistol into the air to frighten people, thereby helping himself and the other accused to flee the scene.
The defense argued that since the appellant did not cause any firearm injuries and no pistol or cartridges were recovered, the conviction was based on mere suspicion.
law: The Court focused on the principles of vicarious liability under Section 149 of the IPC.

Under Section 149, if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, every person who was a member of that assembly at the time is guilty of that offence.
The Court clarified that for a conviction with the aid of Section 149, it is not necessary to prove that a specific accused person committed an 'overt act' (such as causing an injury).
The mere presence of an accused as part of the unlawful assembly is sufficient for conviction under Section 149.
application: The Court found that the eyewitness testimony established that the appellant was a member of the unlawful assembly.
It determined that the common object of this assembly was to murder the deceased ('eliminating Satya Narain').
The appellant's act of firing into the air to facilitate the escape was seen as an act in furtherance of this common object.

The Court dismissed the appellant's defense arguments by applying the law of Section 149. It held that the fact he did not personally cause an injury was irrelevant, as no overt act is required for conviction under this section.
Similarly, the non-recovery of the pistol or cartridges was not considered fatal to the prosecution's case, as his membership in the unlawful assembly was the key element for establishing his guilt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had successfully proven the charges against the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC beyond a reasonable doubt. By being a member of the unlawful assembly with the common object of committing murder, the appellant was held guilty of the murder itself, regardless of his specific role. The Court, therefore, affirmed the convictions by the lower courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a part of the unlawful assembly and if he actually took part in the crime or not.

facts: Eyewitnesses (PW-1 and PW-2) testified that the appellant was part of the group that committed the murder, and their testimony was not shaken during cross-examination.
The appellant performed an overt act by firing his country-made pistol to help the other accused persons escape.
The appellant argued that he should not be convicted because there were no firearm injuries on the victim, and no pistol or empty cartridge was recovered from the scene.
law: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), if an offense is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in pursuit of a common object, every person who is a member of that assembly is guilty of that offense.

The key question for a conviction under Section 149 IPC is whether the accused was a member of the unlawful assembly, not whether they actually took an active part in the crime or personally caused an injury.
Mere presence as part of an unlawful assembly is sufficient for conviction under Section 149 IPC; a specific overt act is not required to be proven against each individual.
application: The Court relied on the credible testimony of two eyewitnesses to establish that the appellant was present and part of the unlawful assembly.
The Court found that the common object of this assembly was to kill the deceased.
The appellant's act of firing his pistol was seen as clear evidence of his participation and shared intent with the group.

The Court dismissed the appellant's arguments regarding the lack of firearm injuries and non-recovery of the weapon as irrelevant. It reasoned that under Section 149 IPC, the focus is on membership in the assembly, not the specific outcome of an individual's actions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was a member of the unlawful assembly that had the common object of committing murder. Therefore, he was held guilty of murder under Sections 302/149 IPC, as his membership in the assembly made him liable for the crime committed by the group, regardless of whether his own actions directly caused injury.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution could prove the charges against the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC beyond reasonable doubt.
appellant_arguments: The appellant has been convicted solely on the basis of suspicion, not hard evidence.
In a criminal trial, if there is an iota of doubt as to the culpability of an accused, he has to be given the benefit of the doubt.
respondent_arguments: The conviction and sentence of the appellant are fully justified and there is no reason to interfere with the same.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was a part of the unlawful assembly and if he actually took part in the crime or not.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's conviction was based on mere suspicion rather than hard evidence, failing to prove his participation.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was very much a part of the unlawful assembly as one of the persons at the place of occurrence.

cases.principle: Section 149 IPC creates a constructive or vicarious liability for members of an unlawful assembly. The factum of causing an injury is not relevant when an accused is roped in with the aid of Section 149 IPC; the relevant question is whether the accused was a member of the unlawful assembly, not whether they actually took an active part in the crime.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain a binding legal rule.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant was a part of an unlawful assembly that had the common object of eliminating the deceased by using criminal force. Consequently, by virtue of being a member of that unlawful assembly, the appellant is also guilty of the murder that was committed in prosecution of the group's common object, and the charges under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC were proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
legal_tests_applied: If an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or such as the members of that assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who, at the time of committing of that offence, is a member of the said assembly; is guilty of that offence. Thus, if it is a case of murder under Section 302 IPC, each member of the unlawful assembly would be guilty of committing the offence under Section 302 IPC.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's mere membership in the unlawful assembly is sufficient for conviction.
The appellant was part of the unlawful assembly which had the common object of eliminating the deceased by criminal force.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution successfully proved that the appellant was a member of the unlawful assembly, which is sufficient to hold him guilty of the murder committed in prosecution of the common object.
The charges against the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 were proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
